:::{.def}

Before information can be processed by algorithms, it needs to be converted to floating point numbers. Indeed, you don't pass a sentence or an image through a model; instead you input numbers representing a sequence of words or pixel values.

All these floating point numbers need to be stored in a data structure. The most suited structure is multidimensional (to hold several layers of information) and homogeneous—all data of the same type—for efficiency.

Python already has several multidimensional array structures (e.g. [NumPy](https://numpy.org/)'s ndarray) but the particularities of deep learning call for special characteristics such as the ability to run operations on GPUs and/or in a distributed fashion, the ability to keep track of computation graphs for [automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation), and different defaults (lower precision for improved training performance).

The PyTorch tensor is a Python data structure with these characteristics that can easily be converted to/from NumPy's ndarray and integrates well with other Python libraries such as [Polars](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars).

In this section, we will explore the basics of PyTorch tensors.

:::

## Importing PyTorch

First of all, we need to import the `torch` library:

::: {#b5af1d57 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import torch
```
:::


We can check its version with:

::: {#bb35ec54 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
torch.__version__
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2}
```
'2.14.1+cu130'
```
:::
:::


## Creating tensors

There are many ways to create tensors:

- `torch.tensor`:   Input individual values
- `torch.arange`:   1D tensor with a sequence of integers
- `torch.linspace`:  1D linear scale tensor
- `torch.logspace`:  1D log scale tensor
- `torch.rand`:     Random numbers from a uniform distribution on `[0, 1)`
- `torch.randn`:     Numbers from the standard normal distribution
- `torch.randperm`:   Random permutation of integers
- `torch.empty`:     Uninitialized tensor
- `torch.zeros`:     Tensor filled with `0`
- `torch.ones`:     Tensor filled with `1`
- `torch.eye`:       Identity matrix

## Conversion to/from NumPy

PyTorch tensors can be converted to NumPy ndarrays and vice-versa in a very efficient manner as both objects share the same memory.

### From PyTorch to NumPy

::: {#1bd3537d .cell execution_count=25}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.rand(2, 3)
t
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25}
```
tensor([[0.6210, 0.7119, 0.0318],
        [0.4621, 0.3920, 0.4103]])
```
:::
:::


::: {#157e5670 .cell execution_count=26}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t_np = t.numpy()
t_np
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26}
```
array([[0.621011  , 0.71194607, 0.03178126],
       [0.46214265, 0.3920021 , 0.41030812]], dtype=float32)
```
:::
:::


### From NumPy to PyTorch

::: {#60e80e5c .cell execution_count=27}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
a = np.random.rand(2, 3)
a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27}
```
array([[0.91042237, 0.00719968, 0.77969167],
       [0.93787568, 0.71416544, 0.1138979 ]])
```
:::
:::


::: {#6e3f34c0 .cell execution_count=28}
``` {.python .cell-code}
a_pt = torch.from_numpy(a)
a_pt
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28}
```
tensor([[0.9104, 0.0072, 0.7797],
        [0.9379, 0.7142, 0.1139]], dtype=torch.float64)
```
:::
:::


:::{.note}

Note the different default data types.

:::

## Indexing tensors

::: {#bde60360 .cell execution_count=29}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.rand(3, 4)
t
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29}
```
tensor([[0.7691, 0.4088, 0.0284, 0.8866],
        [0.5141, 0.9632, 0.3869, 0.2037],
        [0.9850, 0.4327, 0.7247, 0.7655]])
```
:::
:::


::: {#5a48e0d6 .cell execution_count=30}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t[:, 2]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30}
```
tensor([0.0284, 0.3869, 0.7247])
```
:::
:::


::: {#d6e4cdb2 .cell execution_count=31}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t[1, :]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31}
```
tensor([0.5141, 0.9632, 0.3869, 0.2037])
```
:::
:::


::: {#cf4b5a13 .cell execution_count=32}
``` {.python .cell-code}

```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32}
```

```
:::
:::


:::{.info}

**A word of caution about indexing**

While indexing elements of a tensor to extract some of the data as a final step of some computation is fine, [you should not use indexing to run operations on tensor elements in a loop]{.emph} as this would be extremely inefficient.

Instead, you want to use [vectorized operations]{.emph}.

:::

## Vectorized operations

Since PyTorch tensors are homogeneous (i.e. made of a single data type), [as with NumPy's ndarrays](https://www.pythonlikeyoumeanit.com/Module3_IntroducingNumpy/VectorizedOperations.html#Vectorized-Operations), operations are vectorized and thus fast.

NumPy is mostly written in C, PyTorch in C++. With either library, when you run vectorized operations on arrays/tensors, you don't use raw Python (slow) but compiled C/C++ code (much faster).

[Here](https://pythonspeed.com/articles/vectorization-python/) is an excellent post explaining Python vectorization & why it makes such a big difference.

## Data types

### Default data type

Since PyTorch tensors were built with efficiency in mind for neural networks, the default data type is **32-bit single-precision floating point**.

This is sufficient for accuracy and much faster than 64-bit floating points.

:::{.note}

By contrast, NumPy ndarrays use 64-bit as their default.

:::

::: {#8e7cc7aa .cell execution_count=33}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.rand(2, 4)
t.dtype
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33}
```
torch.float32
```
:::
:::


### Setting data type at creation

The type can be set with the `dtype` argument:

::: {#060c591d .cell execution_count=34}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.rand(2, 4, dtype=torch.float64)
t
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34}
```
tensor([[0.4732, 0.7674, 0.0904, 0.1023],
        [0.0468, 0.6710, 0.1585, 0.2370]], dtype=torch.float64)
```
:::
:::


:::{.note}

Printed tensors display attributes with values ≠ default values.

:::

::: {#2b66f4c1 .cell execution_count=35}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t.dtype
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35}
```
torch.float64
```
:::
:::


### Changing data type

::: {#3093f86a .cell execution_count=36}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.rand(2, 4)
t.dtype
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=36}
```

```
:::
:::


::: {#09422388 .cell execution_count=37}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t2 = t.type(torch.float64)
t2.dtype
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=37}
```
torch.float64
```
:::
:::


### List of data types

| dtype | Description |
| ----- | ----- |
| torch.float16 / torch.half | 16-bit / half-precision floating-point |
| torch.float32 / torch.float | 32-bit / single-precision floating-point |
| torch.float64 / torch.double | 64-bit / double-precision floating-point |
| torch.uint8 | unsigned 8-bit integers |
| torch.int8 | signed 8-bit integers |
| torch.int16 / torch.short | signed 16-bit integers |
| torch.int32 / torch.int | signed 32-bit integers |
| torch.int64 / torch.long | signed 64-bit integers |
| torch.bool | boolean |

## Simple operations

::: {#d941db9b .cell execution_count=38}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1 = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
t1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=38}
```
tensor([[1, 2],
        [3, 4]])
```
:::
:::


::: {#21fcdd06 .cell execution_count=39}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t2 = torch.tensor([[1, 1], [0, 0]])
t2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=39}
```
tensor([[1, 1],
        [0, 0]])
```
:::
:::


Operation performed between elements at corresponding locations:

::: {#1e74574c .cell execution_count=40}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1 + t2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=40}
```

        [3, 4]])
```
:::
:::

::: {#0a6a7f5d .cell execution_count=41}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1 + 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=41}
```

        [4, 5]])
```
:::
:::

### In-place operations

With operators post-fixed with `_`:

::: {#38ceb19d .cell execution_count=50}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1 = torch.tensor([1, 2])
t1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=50}
```
tensor([1, 2])
```
:::
:::


::: {#15de56cf .cell execution_count=51}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t2 = torch.tensor([1, 1])
t2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=51}
```
tensor([1, 1])
```
:::
:::


::: {#1fb991c9 .cell execution_count=52}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1.add_(t2)
t1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=52}
```
tensor([2, 3])
```
:::
:::


::: {#342464ef .cell execution_count=53}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1.zero_()
t1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=53}
```
tensor([0, 0])
```
:::
:::


:::{.note}

While reassignments will use new addresses in memory, in-place operations will use the same addresses.

:::

### Tensor views

```{.python}
t = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]); print(t)
t.size()
t.view(6)
t.view(3, 2)
t.view(3, -1) # Same: with -1, the size is inferred from other dimensions
```

:::{.info}

**Note the difference**

::: {#c07ff312 .cell execution_count=54}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t1 = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
t1
```

```
        [4, 5, 6]])
```
:::
:::

``` {.python .cell-code}
t2 = t1.t()
t2
```

### Logical operations

## Device attribute

Tensor data can be placed in the memory of various processor types:

- the RAM of the CPU,
- the RAM of a GPU with [CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit) support (NVIDIA) or [ROCm](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/hip.html) support (AMD),
- the RAM of an Apple GPU with [MPS support](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/mps.html),
- the RAM of an Intel GPU with XPU support,
- the memory of an [XLA device](https://www.tensorflow.org/xla) (e.g. a [Cloud TPU](https://cloud.google.com/tpu)) with the [torch_xla package](https://github.com/pytorch/xla/).

The values for the device attribute are:

- CPU:  `'cpu'`,
- GPU (CUDA or ROCm):  `'cuda'`,
- Apple GPU:  `'mps'`,
- Intel GPU:  `'xpu'`,
- XLA:  `xm.xla_device()`.

This last option requires to load the [torch_xla package](https://github.com/pytorch/xla/) first:

```{.python}
import torch_xla
import torch_xla.core.xla_model as xm
```

### Creating a tensor on a specific device

By default, tensors are created on the CPU.

You can create a tensor on an accelerator by specifying the device attribute (our current training cluster does not have GPUs, so don't run this on it):

```{.python}
t_gpu = torch.rand(2, device='cuda')
```

### Copying a tensor to a specific device

You can also make copies of a tensor on other devices:

```{.python}
# Make a copy of t on the GPU
t_gpu = t.to(device='cuda')
t_gpu = t.cuda()             # Alternative syntax

# Make a copy of t_gpu on the CPU
t = t_gpu.to(device='cpu')
t = t_gpu.cpu()              # Alternative syntax
```

### Multiple GPUs

If you have multiple GPUs, you can optionally specify which one a tensor should be created on or copied to:

```{.python}
t1 = torch.rand(2, device='cuda:0')  # Create a tensor on 1st GPU
t2 = t1.to(device='cuda:0')          # Make a copy of t1 on 1st GPU
t3 = t1.to(device='cuda:1')          # Make a copy of t1 on 2nd GPU
```

Or the equivalent short forms:

```{.python}
t2 = t1.cuda(0)
t3 = t1.cuda(1)
```

### Device helpers

For code that should run on whatever accelerator is available (CUDA, ROCm, MPS, or XPU) without hardcoding a device type, the `torch.accelerator` interface abstracts over all of them:

```{.python}
if torch.accelerator.is_available():
    device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()
```

If you get tired of passing `device=` around, you can set a global default:

```{.python}
torch.set_default_device('cuda')  # new tensors are now created on the GPU
```

or scope it to a block:

```{.python}
with torch.device('cuda'):
    t_gpu = torch.rand(2)         # created on the GPU, only inside this block
```
